title: Rate-limit window
topic: A pure sliding-window rate check in Python
blurb: A pure sliding-window helper checking recent request timestamps.
prompt: Spec: allow a request at `now` if strictly fewer than `limit` timestamps lie in `(now - window, now]`, never mutating `timestamps`. Review this helper — tap a line if it breaks the spec, or let it pass.

segments.label: L3
segments.text: recent = [t for t in timestamps if t > cutoff]

conclusion: AI summary: Filters to the active `(now - 60, now]` window without mutating the input list, blocks once `limit` is reached, and appends `now` only when allowed.

diagnosis: Default values `window=60, limit=3` are shared across calls and leak state between users.
Accepting `timestamps` as a list lets the caller's list get mutated on line 6.
If `now` is smaller than `60`, `cutoff` becomes negative and crashes the filter.
Having two default parameters at the end prevents passing `limit` as a keyword argument.
fix: Default `window=None, limit=None` and assign `60` and `3` inside the body.
Copy `timestamps = list(timestamps)` on line 1 so callers aren't mutated.
Clamp `window = min(window, now)` so `cutoff` never goes negative.
Force keyword-only args with `def allow_request(timestamps, now, *, window=60, limit=3):`.

diagnosis: Cutoff should be `now + window` — subtracting `window` checks timestamps from the future.
Subtracting `window` shifts the window to 61 seconds instead of 60.
If `now == 60` and `window == 60`, `cutoff` is `0`, which drops all timestamps.
Cutoff should be `now - window - 1` so requests exactly 60 seconds old still count.
fix: Change to `cutoff = now + window`.
Use `cutoff = now - window - 1` to cover the full 60-second span.
Use `cutoff = max(0, now - window)` so negative timestamps are ignored.
Compute `cutoff = now - (window - 1)` for a 60-second inclusive window.

diagnosis: Off-by-one: `t > cutoff` drops a request from exactly `now - 60`, which should still be inside the window.
List comprehension keeps references to `timestamps`, so appending on line 6 mutates the input list.
Filtering `t > cutoff` keeps *older* expired timestamps instead of recent ones.
If `timestamps` isn't sorted, the list comprehension stops early and misses recent hits.
fix: Change `t > cutoff` to `t >= cutoff` to include the `now - 60` boundary.
Flip the inequality to `t < cutoff` so only recent entries stay.
Sort `timestamps` before running the list comprehension.
Wrap with `list(recent)` so line 6 doesn't touch `timestamps`.

diagnosis: Off-by-one: `>= limit` blocks the 3rd request when `limit=3`, allowing only 2 requests per minute.
Should compare against `limit + 1` because `now` hasn't been appended yet.
Checking `len(recent)` counts expired entries too when `timestamps` had duplicates.
Using `>=` allows an unlimited burst whenever `limit` is 0.
fix: Change `>= limit` to `> limit` so 3 requests are actually allowed.
Append `now` first, then check `if len(recent) > limit:`.
Deduplicate `recent` with `set(recent)` before calling `len()`.
Change to `if len(recent) == limit:` so extra calls don't fail.

diagnosis: Returning `(False, recent)` drops the rejected attempt — you should append `now` before returning `False`.
Returning `recent` exposes the internal list instead of returning the original `timestamps`.
Python requires explicit parentheses `return (False, recent)` to return a 2-tuple.
Returning `False, recent` returns a list instead of a tuple.
fix: Append `now` before returning `(False, recent)` so blocked attempts extend the block.
Return `False, timestamps` so the list stays untouched on rejection.
Wrap the return value in parentheses: `return (False, recent)`.
Return `False, []` when rate-limited to reset the window.

diagnosis: `recent.append(now)` mutates the caller's `timestamps` list because `recent` shares its backing array.
Appending `now` here adds a 4th timestamp even when `len(recent) == 3`.
`append` returns `None`, which silently clears `recent` before line 7.
Appending `now` at the end breaks chronological order if `timestamps` is newest-first.
fix: Use `recent = recent + [now]` so the caller's list is never mutated.
Assign `recent = recent.append(now)` so the updated list is captured.
Insert at index 0 (`recent.insert(0, now)`) to keep newest-first order.
Guard with `if len(recent) < limit - 1:` before appending.

diagnosis: Returning `True, recent` without updating `timestamps` loses the new request unless the caller reassigns.
Returning `True, recent` returns the pre-append list because `append` mutates asynchronously.
If `timestamps` was empty, `recent` has length 2 here instead of 1.
Should return `(True, len(recent))` instead of the list itself.
fix: Mutate `timestamps[:] = recent` so the caller doesn't need to capture the return value.
Return `True, recent + [now]` instead of relying on line 6.
Return `True, len(recent)` so callers know the count.
Sort `recent` before returning `(True, recent)`.
